passage:
The doctrine of jus cogens — those peremptory norms of international law from which no derogation is permitted — occupies an uneasy position within the architecture of the international legal order. Unlike ordinary treaty obligations, which bind only the states that have consented to them, jus cogens norms are understood to bind all states regardless of consent, a proposition that sits in evident tension with the sovereignty-based foundations upon which the modern state system has rested since the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. For this reason, international tribunals and legal theorists have long debated not merely which norms qualify as peremptory but whether the category is coherent at all, given that the voluntarist tradition insists that international law can derive its force only from the free agreement of sovereign states.

The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, concluded in 1969, gave jus cogens its first formal textual recognition, declaring that any treaty conflicting with a peremptory norm is void ab initio. The Convention, however, did not enumerate which norms rise to this status; it left that determination to the international community, by which it meant, in practice, the jurisprudence of international courts and the writings of publicists. This legislative restraint was deliberate: the drafters feared that any fixed list would calcify prematurely, excluding emerging norms whose claim to peremptory status might be compelling. Yet the very openness of the criteria has generated its own difficulties. States and tribunals have asserted peremptory status for an ever-expanding catalog of norms — ranging from the prohibition of torture and the prohibition of aggression to certain rules of humanitarian law and even, in some scholarly arguments, the principle of permanent sovereignty over natural resources — without offering a principled account of the threshold separating jus cogens from merely ius dispositivum, the ordinary, derogable rules of international law.

The problem is compounded by the relationship between jus cogens and customary international law. Both arise outside the treaty framework; both claim universality. Yet customary international law is, in the traditional account, formed by the convergent practice of states accompanied by opinio juris — the belief that the practice is legally required — and it can be modified by subsequent contrary practice. Jus cogens, by contrast, cannot be modified except by a later norm of the same character. This asymmetry creates a difficult interpretive question: when a state's conduct appears to challenge what one tribunal has treated as a peremptory norm, is that conduct evidence of persistent objection that might erode the norm (as would be possible under ordinary custom) or evidence of a violation of a higher-order rule that no amount of state practice can dislodge? The International Court of Justice has, in several advisory opinions issued since 1970, acknowledged this tension without fully resolving it, preferring cautious formulations that neither entrench a comprehensive catalogue nor foreclose future development.

This judicial reticence is defensible as a matter of institutional prudence, but it exacts a cost. Litigants invoking jus cogens before domestic courts — as occurs with increasing frequency under universal jurisdiction statutes — encounter sovereign immunity defenses that many domestic tribunals are reluctant to pierce, even where the alleged conduct would constitute a clear violation of a candidate peremptory norm. A more forthright judicial elaboration of the criteria for peremptory status, even at the risk of some doctrinal rigidity, would likely produce more consistent outcomes for claimants and would reinforce, rather than undermine, the legitimacy of the norms themselves. One hopes that the International Court of Justice, in adjudicating the wave of cases implicating state responsibility for mass atrocities that has reached its docket in recent years, will supply the conceptual structure that the Vienna Convention's drafters were unwilling to provide.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties failed to define jus cogens with sufficient precision, and this failure has allowed states to invoke the doctrine to invalidate inconvenient treaty obligations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of jus cogens is theoretically incoherent because it cannot be reconciled with the voluntarist foundations of international law and should therefore be abandoned.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The undefined boundaries of jus cogens, combined with courts' reluctance to elaborate the doctrine, produce inconsistent legal outcomes, and a more rigorous judicial articulation of peremptory norms is needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: International courts have consistently expanded the catalogue of jus cogens norms in ways that undermine state sovereignty and destabilize customary international law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The distinction between jus cogens and customary international law is illusory, since both categories claim universality and neither can be modified by ordinary state practice.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the theoretical tension around jus cogens (¶1), the indeterminacy left by the Vienna Convention (¶2), the unresolved relationship with customary law (¶3), and culminates in the author's prescription that courts should more forthrightly elaborate peremptory criteria (¶4). C captures this arc — indeterminate doctrine + judicial reticence → inconsistent outcomes → call for clearer articulation.
explanations.A: Too narrow; the passage's concern is not that states exploit the doctrine to void treaties but rather that the lack of criteria creates systemic inconsistency across tribunals and domestic courts.
explanations.B: The author does not call for abandoning jus cogens; this choice overstates the voluntarist critique as the author's own view rather than a theoretical challenge the author acknowledges.
explanations.D: The passage says courts have been cautious and reticent, not that they have systematically expanded the catalogue; this choice inverts the passage's characterization of judicial behavior.
explanations.E: The author distinguishes the two doctrines (modifiability is the key asymmetry) rather than collapsing them; this choice misrepresents the argument of ¶3.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the International Court of Justice's handling of jus cogens doctrine can best be described as which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unqualified admiration for the Court's restraint in avoiding premature doctrinal commitments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sympathetic understanding of the Court's caution, tempered by regret that its reticence imposes practical costs on litigants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Outright condemnation of the Court for its deliberate evasion of a difficult but tractable legal question.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skepticism that the Court possesses the institutional competence necessary to elaborate a coherent doctrine of peremptory norms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Approval of the Court's advisory opinions as models of careful jurisprudential reasoning under conditions of doctrinal uncertainty.

explanations.correct: The author concedes that 'judicial reticence is defensible as a matter of institutional prudence' (acknowledging the Court's position) but immediately notes it 'exacts a cost' (practical harm to litigants), and closes with 'one hopes' that the Court will supply the needed structure — a tone of measured disappointment rather than wholesale condemnation or admiration.
explanations.A: The author explicitly qualifies approval with a 'but it exacts a cost' — unqualified admiration is contradicted by the passage's fourth paragraph.
explanations.C: 'Outright condemnation' overstates the author's tone; the author accepts that caution is institutionally defensible and uses guarded hope rather than accusatory language.
explanations.D: The author expresses no doubt about the Court's competence; the prescription 'one hopes' implies the author believes the Court is capable of the task.
explanations.E: The author describes the ICJ's formulations as 'cautious' and says they neither 'entrench a comprehensive catalogue nor foreclose future development,' which is a neutral-to-critical observation, not approval of the opinions as models.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A foundational theoretical tension is introduced; a landmark legal instrument that addressed but did not resolve the tension is examined; an additional complication arising from the relationship between two legal doctrines is analyzed; and a prescription for resolving the resulting practical problem is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; its historical origins are traced from antiquity to the present; a series of failed attempts by international courts to apply it are described; and an alternative approach drawn from domestic law is proposed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A controversial scholarly argument is introduced; evidence for and against it is presented from treaty law and customary law; the argument is ultimately rejected; and a less controversial replacement principle is endorsed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two competing conceptions of international legal obligation are contrasted; their respective advantages and disadvantages are weighed; one is endorsed as theoretically superior; and the other is identified as the source of a contemporary legal problem.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A legal doctrine's practical applications are surveyed; a problem of inconsistent judicial interpretation is identified; the historical causes of that inconsistency are traced; and a procedural reform to correct the inconsistency is recommended.

explanations.correct: ¶1 presents the foundational tension (jus cogens vs. voluntarist sovereignty); ¶2 examines the Vienna Convention's contribution and residual indeterminacy; ¶3 analyzes the complication arising from the relationship between jus cogens and customary law; ¶4 argues that judicial reticence has practical costs and prescribes more forthright elaboration.
explanations.B: The passage does not trace historical origins from antiquity, and no 'alternative approach drawn from domestic law' is proposed — the prescription calls for the ICJ to act, not for importing a domestic-law solution.
explanations.C: No single 'controversial scholarly argument' is introduced and then rejected; the passage is a structural analysis of doctrinal difficulties, not a rebuttal of a specific scholarly thesis.
explanations.D: The passage does not weigh two conceptions and endorse one; both jus cogens and customary law are presented as coexisting but imperfectly reconciled elements of the same system.
explanations.E: The historical causes traced in the passage are doctrinal, not 'causes of inconsistent interpretation' in the procedural sense; furthermore, no 'procedural reform' is recommended — the prescription concerns substantive doctrinal elaboration.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the drafters of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties deliberately refrained from enumerating specific jus cogens norms primarily because they

choices.label: A
choices.text: could not reach consensus on which norms had achieved sufficient state practice to qualify as customary international law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: wished to preserve state sovereignty by ensuring that individual states retained the right to object to proposed peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: feared that enumerating norms would freeze the category too early and might exclude later norms with a strong claim to peremptory status.

choices.label: D
choices.text: believed that the International Court of Justice was better positioned to compile such a list through its advisory jurisdiction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: anticipated that state practice would eventually generate a widely accepted catalogue of norms without any formal legal specification.

explanations.correct: The passage states directly: 'the drafters feared that any fixed list would calcify prematurely, excluding emerging norms whose claim to peremptory status might be compelling.' C is a close paraphrase of this.
explanations.A: The passage does not mention a failure to reach consensus on customary-law thresholds; the concern was about premature calcification, not drafting disagreement.
explanations.B: The passage nowhere attributes the drafters' restraint to a desire to protect state sovereignty; the voluntarist objection is the author's framing of the theoretical tension, not the drafters' motivation.
explanations.D: The passage says the determination was left to 'the jurisprudence of international courts and the writings of publicists,' but it does not specifically say the drafters believed the ICJ's advisory jurisdiction was better suited — this is an inference the passage does not support.
explanations.E: The passage does not suggest the drafters expected state practice alone to produce a catalogue; the open criteria were a deliberate choice to allow organic development, but no such specific expectation is attributed to the drafters.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that which one of the following is true of customary international law, as the author understands it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot bind states that have persistently objected to a given norm during the period of its formation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is inferior to treaty law in normative rank because it lacks the explicit consent of the states it purports to bind.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It may be altered over time by subsequent contrary state practice, whereas jus cogens norms may not be so altered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It arises exclusively from the decisions of international courts and the scholarly writings of publicists.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is rendered obsolete wherever a treaty norm addressing the same subject matter has entered into force.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states that customary international law 'can be modified by subsequent contrary practice,' whereas jus cogens 'cannot be modified except by a later norm of the same character.' C directly follows from this contrast.
explanations.A: The passage mentions 'persistent objection' as a possibility that could erode ordinary custom, but it does not affirmatively state the rule that persistent objectors are not bound — this is an inference beyond what the passage directly supports.
explanations.B: The passage does not establish any normative hierarchy between customary law and treaty law; the hierarchy discussed is between jus cogens and ius dispositivum (ordinary rules, which include both treaties and custom).
explanations.D: The passage says customary international law is 'formed by the convergent practice of states accompanied by opinio juris' — state practice and belief, not court decisions or scholarly writings, which are instead cited as the source for identifying jus cogens norms.
explanations.E: The passage makes no claim that treaty law displaces customary law on the same subject; the lex specialis principle is not discussed.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to universal jurisdiction statutes in the fourth paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate a specific domestic-law mechanism through which the practical consequences of judicial reticence about jus cogens most acutely affect individual litigants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that domestic courts, rather than international tribunals, are better suited to resolve disputes implicating peremptory norms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that the expansion of universal jurisdiction has itself caused the indeterminacy in the jus cogens catalogue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the robust enforcement mechanisms available in domestic law with the weaker remedial capacity of international courts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide a historical example of how state practice under universal jurisdiction statutes has contributed to the formation of customary international law.

explanations.correct: The reference to universal jurisdiction statutes appears immediately after the author states that judicial reticence 'exacts a cost,' and it specifies the setting where that cost is most visible: litigants in domestic courts invoking jus cogens face sovereign immunity defenses. The reference concretizes the abstract harm described in the preceding sentence.
explanations.B: The author does not argue domestic courts are better suited than international tribunals; if anything, the prescription is for the ICJ to supply the conceptual structure that would help domestic courts apply the doctrine consistently.
explanations.C: The passage does not suggest that universal jurisdiction statutes caused the indeterminacy; the indeterminacy stems from the Vienna Convention's drafting choice and the absence of judicial elaboration.
explanations.D: No contrast between domestic and international remedial capacity is drawn; the point is that domestic courts face a specific obstacle (sovereign immunity) that results from the lack of clear doctrinal elaboration.
explanations.E: No historical narrative about universal jurisdiction and customary law formation is offered; the reference is functional, not historical.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that a more forthright judicial articulation of jus cogens criteria would produce more consistent outcomes for claimants invoking peremptory norms before domestic courts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several states that are parties to the Vienna Convention have enacted domestic legislation explicitly incorporating the jus cogens provisions of that treaty into their national legal systems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sovereign immunity defenses that domestic courts apply in jus cogens cases are grounded in statutes that domestic courts lack authority to override regardless of how clearly a peremptory norm has been judicially defined.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The International Court of Justice has in recent years accepted jurisdiction over a significant number of cases involving alleged state responsibility for mass atrocities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Legal scholars disagree substantially about whether any norm beyond the prohibition of genocide has achieved the threshold of universal acceptance necessary for peremptory status.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Domestic courts in states with monist legal systems have been more willing than those in dualist systems to apply jus cogens norms directly without requiring domestic implementing legislation.

explanations.correct: The author argues that clearer judicial articulation of jus cogens would help litigants in domestic courts by enabling those courts to pierce sovereign immunity defenses more readily. If, however, sovereign immunity is grounded in statutory law that domestic courts cannot override regardless of doctrinal clarity, then clearer ICJ articulation would not produce the consistent outcomes the author envisions. B directly cuts the causal link between the proposed remedy and the claimed benefit.
explanations.A: Domestic legislation incorporating Vienna Convention provisions would tend to support, not undermine, the author's prescription; it suggests domestic implementation of international law norms is feasible.
explanations.C: The ICJ's acceptance of more cases is consistent with the author's hope and neither strengthens nor weakens the specific causal claim about domestic-court outcomes.
explanations.D: Scholarly disagreement about the threshold for peremptory status is evidence of the doctrinal uncertainty the author already acknowledges, but it does not directly address whether clearer judicial articulation would improve domestic-court outcomes — it bears on whether such articulation is possible, not whether it would be effective.
explanations.E: The difference between monist and dualist systems is an additional variable but does not undermine the author's causal claim; the author's prescription would still improve outcomes in monist systems even if dualist systems remained resistant.
